item.title: 25-year-old says children are not bullocks to be beaten into obedience
item.description: A 25-year-old youth Nitish Sharma says children are not bullocks and cannot be beaten into obedience, raising concerns about the chastisement of children during the consultation on the Constitution Amendment Bill in Suva. Sharma, who is originally from Cuvu, Sigatoka, says although children may not always listen to their parents and teachers, physical punishment is not the solution.
item.content:encoded:
A 25-year-old youth Nitish Sharma says children are not bullocks and cannot be beaten into obedience, raising concerns about the chastisement of children during the consultation on the Constitution Amendment Bill in Suva.

Sharma, who is originally from Cuvu, Sigatoka, says although children may not always listen to their parents and teachers, physical punishment is not the solution.

He says issues such as drugs and HIV are concerning, but beating children will not necessarily change their behaviour.

Insert:Sharma on chastisement of children nb 15th Oct

He also raises concerns about several other proposed constitutional changes, including immunity provisions, saying it is time for the country to move forward, learn from the past and focus on preventing similar violations in the future.

Sharma questions the need for a Senate, arguing that Parliament should be strong enough to prevent unnecessary bills from being passed.

He also questions the process of repeatedly sending bills between the two chambers and says Senate members should be elected rather than appointed.

Sharma says Fiji is a diverse country and all communities should have an opportunity to be represented in Parliament.

On the selection of the President, he says Parliament should elect the Head of State rather than leaving the decision solely to a group of people.

He acknowledges the role of chiefs but questions whether they should be the only ones deciding who becomes President.

Sharma also calls for the current four-year parliamentary term to remain, rather than being extended to five years.

He says people should continue to have a say in future constitutional amendments through referendums, arguing that the Constitution belongs to the people and they should not be excluded from decisions about it.

On the electoral system, Sharma supports retaining the current single nationwide open-list system, saying it allows voters to choose candidates regardless of where they live.

He questions whether a constituency-based system could restrict voters to candidates from their own areas and raises concerns about how electoral boundaries and seats would be allocated, particularly for outer islands and other communities.

Sharma says the electoral system should ensure votes are fairly represented and that people have a genuine choice in who represents them.

item.title: Takayawa describes use of Fijian as national identity under 2013 Constitution as technical genocide
item.description: Former SODELPA General Secretary Viliame Takayawa describes the use of 'Fijian' as a national identity under the 2013 Constitution as 'technical genocide', saying it has taken away part of the indigenous people's history and identity. Takayawa made the comments during public consultation on the Constitution Amendment Bill, where he raised concerns about the national identity introduced under the 2
item.content:encoded:
Former SODELPA General Secretary Viliame Takayawa describes the use of 'Fijian' as a national identity under the 2013 Constitution as 'technical genocide', saying it has taken away part of the indigenous people's history and identity.

Takayawa made the comments during public consultation on the Constitution Amendment Bill, where he raised concerns about the national identity introduced under the 2013 Constitution.

He says the term 'Fijian' was historically used to identify the indigenous people of Fiji and believes its use as a national identity has taken away something important from them.

Takayawa says removing the term from its previous use also means deleting part of the history and heritage of indigenous people and their ancestors.

He describes this as 'technical genocide', explaining that he believes genocide can involve not only the killing of people but also the removal of a group's history and identity.

Takayawa also refers to discussions held in 1997, saying the term Fiji Islander was proposed as a national identity that could be shared by all citizens.

He says he believes this would have been a democratic approach to national identity.

Takayawa maintains that indigenous identity should still be recognised, suggesting that an indigenous name could be retained alongside the national identity.

He also says people across the region share a Pacific Islander identity, while reiterating his support for the recognition of Fiji Islanders.

His submission focuses on the relationship between national identity, indigenous heritage and the recognition of the history of Fiji's people.

item.title: Tikaram questions immunity provisions and calls for protection of Indo-Fijians
item.description: Lami resident Tarun Tikaram has questioned the immunity provisions in the proposed Constitution amendments, calling for accountability for wrongdoing and stronger protections for Fijians of Indian descent. Speaking during the consultation on the Constitution Amendment Bill, Tikaram says if people are found to have done something wrong, they should be subject to litigation or prosecution rather tha
item.content:encoded:
Lami resident Tarun Tikaram has questioned the immunity provisions in the proposed Constitution amendments, calling for accountability for wrongdoing and stronger protections for Fijians of Indian descent.

Speaking during the consultation on the Constitution Amendment Bill, Tikaram says if people are found to have done something wrong, they should be subject to litigation or prosecution rather than simply being told not to repeat their actions.

He questions the point of allowing immunity while expecting the country to move forward through reconciliation.

Tikaram also calls for more time to review the proposed Constitution Amendment bill, saying the Constitution is an important document that should not be rushed.

He says people must have the opportunity to understand the document, take ownership of it and uphold its provisions.

He also questioned the legal process for holding a referendum, asking whether the Prime Minister has the authority to call for one, set its date or direct the Electoral Commission to conduct it.

Tikaram urges the committee to carefully examine the relevant laws to avoid potential legal challenges, while asking members to verify whether his interpretation of the process was correct.

He further calls for stronger protections for people born in Fiji, saying he wants everyone to have a sense of belonging and feel that their identity as Fijians is respected.

Insert: Tikaram on hate received 15th Oct Tikaram says he believes iTaukei land and interests are protected through existing laws and institutions,and called for greater consideration of protections for Fijians of Indian Decent.

Prime Minisiter and Joint Parliamentary Select Committee Chair Sitiveni Rabuka says written submissions will be summarised and considered as it reviews the proposed amendments, with some provisions potentially amended depending on the feedback received.

item.title: Turaga remains tight-lipped on widely circulated video, says he will speak after process is completed
item.description: Former Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga says he will not comment on the widely circulated video until all processes are completed. Turaga made the comment when asked whether he had reported the video to the Online Safety Commission, given that it was being widely circulated by some members of the public.
item.content:encoded:
Former Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga says he will not comment on the widely circulated video until all processes are completed.

Turaga made the comment when asked whether he had reported the video to the Online Safety Commission, given that it was being widely circulated by some members of the public.

He was also asked whether his account had been hacked or whether the post was accidental.

Turaga declined to provide further details, saying he would not make any comment for now.

He says he will be able to comment once all the processes are completed.

Turaga has still not clarified whether the video issue has been reported to the Online Safety Commission.

item.title: Cultural barriers make cancer discussions difficult for Lau women - Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau President
item.description: Women from the Lau Islands are being encouraged to undergo regular health checks and seek early medical attention, as cultural barriers continue to make discussions about cancer difficult. Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau President Rigieta Halofaki says many women are reluctant to visit hospitals for check-ups, prompting the organisation to invite representatives from the Fiji Cancer Society and the Min
item.content:encoded:
Women from the Lau Islands are being encouraged to undergo regular health checks and seek early medical attention, as cultural barriers continue to make discussions about cancer difficult.

Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau President Rigieta Halofaki says many women are reluctant to visit hospitals for check-ups, prompting the organisation to invite representatives from the Fiji Cancer Society and the Ministry of Health to raise awareness about cancer affecting women.

Speaking during the the celebration of International Rural Women's Day, Pinktober and Senior Citizens and Expo at the Seafarers Club in Walu Bay, Suva, Halofaki says the awareness sessions aim to help women understand what steps to take if they develop cancer.

She says breast and cervical cancer are among the conditions affecting women in Lau, although the organisation does not have data on the number of women affected.

Halofaki says discussing these health issues can be difficult within Fijian traditions, but awareness programmes provide an opportunity to share information and encourage women to seek medical help.

She says the celebration today also recognises elderly women and senior citizens for their years of service and contribution to Soqosoqo Vakamarama Ko Lau.

Halofaki says the organisation is also working on its strategic development plan, which focuses on rural development, education and preserving traditional Lauan handicrafts.

She says the plan has been revised to combine eight previous thematic areas into five, with a focus on supporting women from the islands and those living in Suva.

Halofaki says preserving traditional handicrafts is important as more companies commercialise such products.

She adds that education remains a priority for the organisation, which wants younger generations to continue pursuing educational opportunities.

Halofaki adds that the Women's Fund Fiji has supported the organisation's work over the past three years, while other activities are funded through fundraising and contributions from women in the different tikinas .
